los.text: Recall the plan and tasks for the week
los.html:
Week 202 overview
  • Three themes.
  • (1) Puberty: normal physiology, precocious and delayed puberty, adolescent psychology, reproductive/renal embryology.
  • (2) Prematurity: clinical course by gestation, fluid/nutrition, infection, ethics at the margins of viability, impact on families.
  • (3) ICM: sexual history and safeguarding, ophthalmology examination, paediatric history (triadic consultation, urinary frequency).
TasksCase presentation, expert forums (puberty; clinicians and families of ex-premature children), anatomy/embryology session, ICM practice.

los.text: Describe the physiology of normal puberty in males and females
los.html:
Trigger
  • Reactivation of the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator (kisspeptin/KISS1R signalling; permissive signals: leptin/adequate body fat, genetics)
  • → pulsatile GnRH
  • → LH and FSH (initially at night)
  • → gonadal sex steroids (gonadarche).
  • Separate adrenarche (adrenal androgens, DHEAS, from ~6–8 yrs) → body odour, pubic/axillary hair.
Girls (onset 8–13)
  • Thelarche (breast bud, Tanner B2) first
  • → pubarche
  • → growth spurt early (peak height velocity ~11.5, at B2–3)
  • → menarche ~12–13 (~2–2.5 yrs after thelarche; at B4).
  • Oestrogen: breast, uterus, fat distribution, epiphyseal fusion.
Boys (onset 9–14)
  • Testicular enlargement ≥4 mL (Prader orchidometer; G2) first
  • → pubic hair
  • → penile growth
  • → growth spurt later (peak ~13.5, at G4)
  • → voice breaking, facial hair, muscle mass
  • Spermarche.
  • Testosterone (and oestrogen via aromatisation closes growth plates).
Tanner staging (1–5)Breasts (girls), genitalia (boys), pubic hair (both).
Growth
  • GH + IGF-1 rise (sex steroids amplify) → growth spurt
  • Final height ~2 yrs after menarche
  • Boys taller due to later spurt (more pre-pubertal growth).
Normal variantsPremature thelarche (isolated, infants), premature adrenarche, pubertal gynaecomastia (boys, common, resolves).

los.text: Describe early puberty, recognise common causes and describe treatment
los.html:
• Precocious puberty: signs before 8 (girls) or 9 (boys).
TypeMechanismCauses
Central (gonadotropin-dependent, "true")Early activation of HPG axis; ↑ LH/FSH, consonant sequence of puberty
  • Girls: mostly idiopathic (~90%)
  • Boys: often pathological: CNS tumours (hypothalamic hamartoma, glioma), hydrocephalus, cranial irradiation, trauma, infection, severe hypothyroidism, adoption/international migration
Peripheral (gonadotropin-independent)Sex steroids from elsewhere; ↓ LH/FSH
  • CAH (boys: small testes with virilisation)
  • Adrenal/gonadal tumours (unilateral testicular enlargement = Leydig cell tumour)
  • McCune–Albright (café-au-lait, fibrous dysplasia, ovarian cysts)
  • hCG-secreting tumours
  • Exogenous steroids
Assessment
  • Growth chart (height velocity ↑), Tanner staging, testicular volumes, neuro exam, skin.
  • Bone age (X-ray left hand; advanced)
  • LH/FSH (± GnRH stimulation test)
  • Oestradiol/testosterone
  • TFTs
  • 17-OH progesterone
  • β-hCG
  • AFP
  • Pelvic USS (uterine/ovarian size)
  • MRI brain (all boys, girls <6 or neurological signs).
Treatment
  • Treat cause
  • Central → GnRH agonist (e.g. leuprorelin/triptorelin depot: continuous stimulation downregulates pituitary) to halt progression, preserve final height and for psychosocial reasons
  • Stop at appropriate age.
  • Psychological support.
ConsequencesReduced final adult height (early epiphyseal fusion), psychosocial difficulties, early menarche.

los.text: Describe delayed puberty, recognise common causes and describe treatment
los.html:
• Delayed puberty: no signs by 13 (girls) or 14 (boys)
    • or no menarche by 15/within 3 yrs of thelarche
    • or arrested progression.
TypeCauses
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)
  • Commonest (especially boys)
  • FHx of late bloomers
  • Short for age but normal height velocity
  • Delayed bone age
  • Normal eventual puberty and height
Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadismChronic disease (IBD, coeliac, CF, CKD, sickle cell), undernutrition/anorexia nervosa, excessive exercise (athletes), hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinaemia, stress
Permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (↓ LH/FSH)Kallmann syndrome (GnRH deficiency + anosmia), pituitary tumours (craniopharyngioma), panhypopituitarism, post-radiotherapy, Prader–Willi
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (↑ LH/FSH; gonadal failure)
  • Turner syndrome (45,X) (short, webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, coarctation, streak ovaries)
  • Klinefelter (47,XXY) (tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia; often presents with arrested puberty)
  • Chemotherapy/radiotherapy
  • Gonadal torsion/orchitis
  • Androgen insensitivity (primary amenorrhoea)
IxGrowth charts, bone age, FBC, U&E, CRP/ESR, coeliac serology, TFTs, prolactin, LH/FSH, testosterone/oestradiol, karyotype, MRI pituitary, smell testing.
Treatment
  • Treat cause
  • CDGP: reassurance ± short course of low-dose testosterone (boys) or oestrogen (girls) to "kick-start" puberty
  • Permanent hypogonadism → lifelong sex-steroid replacement (gradual increase to mimic puberty), fertility treatment (gonadotropins) later
  • Turner: GH + oestrogen
  • Psychological support (bullying, self-esteem).

los.text: Describe the neuropsychological changes and phases of psychological development occurring during adolescence.
los.html:
Adolescence(~10–24 yrs)Transition from childhood to adulthood: biological (puberty), psychological, social.
Brain development
  • Synaptic pruning and myelination continue into mid-20s.
  • Limbic system (reward, emotion; dopaminergic) matures early at puberty, while the prefrontal cortex (executive function, impulse control, planning, risk evaluation) matures later
  • → "maturational imbalance" (dual systems model)
  • → ↑ risk-taking, sensation-seeking, sensitivity to peers and reward, emotional reactivity
  • Heightened neuroplasticity (opportunity and vulnerability).
PhasesEarly (10–13: puberty, concrete thinking, body image concerns), middle (14–17: peer focus, identity exploration, risk-taking, separation from parents, abstract thinking), late (18–24: consolidated identity, intimacy, future orientation).
Theories
  • Erikson – identity vs role confusion
  • Piaget – formal operational thought (abstract, hypothetical reasoning)
  • Elkind – adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable: "it won't happen to me")
  • Marcia's identity statuses.
Clinical relevance
  • ~75% of adult mental illness starts before 24 (anxiety, depression, eating disorders, psychosis, self-harm)
  • Substance use
  • Sexual health
  • Non-adherence in chronic disease (diabetes control worsens)
  • Transition from paediatric to adult services.
Approach
  • HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment (Home, Education/Employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety)
  • See alone for part of consultation
  • Confidentiality (and its limits)
  • Non-judgemental
  • Gillick competence.

los.text: Name the parts of the developing urinary system, and identify the processes of formation of this system.
sessions: Embryology of the reproductive & renal systems
los.html:
• Intermediate mesoderm (urogenital ridge) gives three successive kidney systems (cranial → caudal):
  • Pronephros (week 4): rudimentary, non-functional, regresses.
  • Mesonephros (weeks 4–8): temporary functioning kidney; mesonephric (Wolffian) duct persists → in males forms epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct.
  • Metanephros (from week 5) = permanent kidney: ureteric bud (outgrowth of mesonephric duct) → collecting system (ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, collecting ducts); metanephric blastema (mesenchyme) → nephrons (glomerulus → DCT). Reciprocal induction (GDNF–RET, WT1). Functional from ~week 10–12 (fetal urine → amniotic fluid).
AscentKidneys start in pelvis and ascend to lumbar position, taking new arterial supply (accessory renal arteries common).
Bladder/urethra
  • Cloaca divided by urorectal septum → urogenital sinus (anterior; bladder, urethra) and anorectal canal (posterior).
  • Allantois → urachus → median umbilical ligament.
Anomalies
  • Renal agenesis (bilateral → Potter sequence: oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, facial features)
  • Horseshoe kidney (fused lower poles trapped under IMA; Turner syndrome)
  • Pelvic kidney
  • Duplex kidney/ureter (bifid ureteric bud)
  • PUJ obstruction
  • Posterior urethral valves (boys)
  • Multicystic dysplastic kidney
  • Vesicoureteric reflux
  • Urachal remnants (fistula/cyst: umbilical discharge)
  • Polycystic kidney disease.

los.text: Identify the parts of the developing reproductive systems in male and female embryos, and identify the processes by which the adult structures develop.
sessions: Embryology of the reproductive & renal systems
los.html:
Indifferent stage (to ~week 7)
  • Gonadal ridges (intermediate mesoderm + coelomic epithelium) colonised by primordial germ cells migrating from yolk sac wall
  • Two duct systems in both sexes: mesonephric (Wolffian) and paramesonephric (Müllerian).
Male(SRY on Y → SOX9 → testis)
  • Sertoli cells → anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) → Müllerian ducts regress.
  • Leydig cells → testosterone → Wolffian ducts → epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct.
  • Testosterone → DHT (5α-reductase) → external genitalia: genital tubercle → penis; urogenital folds fuse → penile urethra; labioscrotal swellings → scrotum; prostate.
  • Testicular descent: gubernaculum guides testis via inguinal canal into scrotum (weeks ~25–35); processus vaginalis (→ tunica vaginalis; patent → hernia/hydrocele).
Female(no SRY → ovary; no AMH, no testosterone)
  • Müllerian ducts → fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, upper ⅓ vagina (fusion of caudal ducts; lower vagina from urogenital sinus/sinovaginal bulbs).
  • Wolffian ducts regress (remnants: Gartner's duct cysts).
  • Genital tubercle → clitoris; urogenital folds → labia minora; labioscrotal swellings → labia majora.
  • Ovary descends to pelvis (gubernaculum → ovarian ligament + round ligament).
Anomalies
  • Hypospadias (incomplete fusion of urogenital folds)
  • Cryptorchidism
  • CAH (virilised female)
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY, testes, female external genitalia, no uterus)
  • 5α-reductase deficiency
  • Müllerian anomalies (bicornuate/septate uterus, MRKH syndrome: vaginal/uterine agenesis)
  • Inguinal hernia.

los.text: Discuss the normal and the potential problems that can arise during puberty and adolescence
los.html:
Normal adolescent experiencesPhysical changes and body image concerns, identity exploration, emotional variability, ↑ independence and conflict with parents, peer influence, romantic/sexual relationships, academic pressures.
Potential problems
  • Puberty-related: precocious/delayed puberty, short/tall stature, gynaecomastia, acne, menstrual problems (menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea, PCOS), body image dissatisfaction.
  • Mental health: anxiety, depression, self-harm, eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia; peak onset adolescence), early psychosis, ADHD/ASD challenges.
  • Risk behaviours: alcohol, smoking/vaping, drugs, unsafe sex (STIs, teenage pregnancy), road traffic accidents, violence.
  • Social/safeguarding: bullying/cyberbullying, social media harms, child sexual exploitation, county lines, domestic abuse, gender identity questions.
  • Chronic illness: worsening adherence (T1DM, asthma, epilepsy), transition to adult services, impact on schooling and identity.
Clinicians' role
  • Adolescent-friendly services
  • See alone
  • Confidentiality explained
  • HEEADSSS screening
  • Gillick/Fraser
  • Brief interventions
  • Safeguarding
  • Involve school/CAMHS
  • Health promotion (HPV vaccine, contraception)
  • Structured transition planning (e.g. "Ready Steady Go").

los.text: Identify the challenges of fluid and nutritional management in the preterm infant
los.html:
Fluid challenges
  • Immature skin (thin, poorly keratinised) → huge insensible water losses (especially <28 weeks, under radiant warmers) → use humidified incubators, plastic wraps.
  • Immature kidneys: ↓ GFR, poor concentrating and diluting ability, Na⁺ wasting (later), poor acid excretion → risk of both hyper- and hyponatraemia, fluid overload (PDA, BPD, NEC risk) or dehydration.
  • Postnatal diuresis and weight loss (5–15%) in first days is normal.
  • Typical fluids start ~60–90 mL/kg/day, increasing to ~150–180 mL/kg/day; monitor weight, U&E, glucose, urine output frequently.
  • Glucose: limited glycogen stores and immature gluconeogenesis → hypoglycaemia; also hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance, stress) in extreme preterms.
  • Electrolyte issues: hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia (non-oliguric), metabolic bone disease (↓ Ca/PO₄).
Nutritional challenges
  • High requirements for growth (~110–135 kcal/kg/day, protein 3.5–4 g/kg/day) but immature gut (poor motility, ↓ enzymes), weak suck–swallow–breathe coordination (until ~32–34 weeks) → nasogastric/orogastric feeds.
  • Parenteral nutrition (via central/UVC line) early in very preterm babies → line sepsis, cholestasis, metabolic complications.
  • Breast milk (mother's own, or donor) preferred: ↓ NEC, ↓ infection; fortified with breast milk fortifier for protein/minerals.
  • Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC): risk with formula, rapid feed advancement → bilious aspirates, distension, bloody stools, pneumatosis intestinalis → stop feeds, antibiotics, surgery.
  • Micronutrients: iron (from ~4–6 weeks), vitamin D, phosphate (metabolic bone disease of prematurity).
  • Growth monitoring on preterm charts; postnatal growth restriction affects neurodevelopment.

los.text: Describe the ethics of medical care at the margins of viability
sessions: Ethics at the margin of viability
los.html:
Margins of viability
  • ~22–24 weeks' gestation
  • Survival rises steeply each week (22 wks ~25–30% with active care, 24 wks ~60–70%, 25 wks ~75%), with significant risk of severe disability among survivors.
BAPM framework (2019)
  • Risk-based assessment
  • Not gestation alone: gestation
  • Birthweight/estimated fetal weight
  • Antenatal steroids
  • Sex (girls better)
  • Singleton vs multiple
  • Place of birth (tertiary NICU)
  • Fetal condition.
  • Extremely high risk (e.g. 22+0 with poor factors): palliative (comfort) care recommended, active treatment generally not in best interests.
  • High risk (22–23 weeks): either survival-focused or palliative care may be appropriate, shared decision with parents.
  • Moderate risk (24+ weeks): survival-focused care usually recommended.
Ethical principles
  • Best interests of the baby (paramount), weighing burdens (painful interventions, prolonged intensive care, disability) vs benefits
  • Parental autonomy/role in decision-making as surrogates
  • Sanctity of life vs quality of life
  • Uncertainty of prognosis
  • Justice (resource use)
  • Acts vs omissions
  • Withholding vs withdrawing treatment (ethically equivalent)
  • Professional conscience.
  • No obligation to provide treatment that is not in the baby's best interests (Nuffield Council 2006).
Law
  • The fetus has no legal personality until born alive
  • Abortion Act limit of 24 weeks (debate on consistency)
  • Disputes → courts (e.g. Charlie Gard; best interests).
Practice
  • Early senior counselling (obstetric + neonatal) before birth, honest information, antenatal steroids, magnesium sulfate, birth in a centre with NICU
  • Palliative care pathways (comfort, memory-making, bereavement support)
  • Reassess decisions as situation changes.

los.text: Explain the typical clinical course of premature infants of different gestational age groups including problems in each physiological system
sessions: Case presentation: the spectrum of prematurity
los.html:
GestationTypical course and problems
Extremely preterm (<28 wks)
  • Highest risk: RDS (surfactant deficiency) → ventilation/surfactant
  • Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) (germinal matrix, first 72 h)
  • PDA
  • NEC
  • Late-onset sepsis (lines)
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (O₂ need at 36 wks)
  • Retinopathy of prematurity (screening, laser/anti-VEGF)
  • Apnoea of prematurity (caffeine)
  • Hypothermia
  • Hypo/hyperglycaemia
  • Jaundice
  • Anaemia (transfusions)
  • Periventricular leukomalacia → cerebral palsy
  • Long NICU stay (~until term)
Very preterm (28–31+6)
  • Similar but less severe: RDS (CPAP ± surfactant)
  • Apnoea
  • Feeding difficulties
  • Jaundice
  • Sepsis
  • NEC risk
  • ROP screening if <32 wks or <1501 g
Moderate/late preterm (32–36+6)Often underestimated: feeding difficulties (poor suck), hypoglycaemia, jaundice, temperature instability, transient tachypnoea, mild respiratory distress; readmissions; subtle long-term learning difficulties
  • By system: Resp (RDS, apnoea, BPD)
    • CVS (PDA, hypotension)
    • CNS (IVH, PVL, seizures)
    • GI (feeding intolerance, NEC)
    • Renal (fluid/electrolytes)
    • Metabolic (glucose, bone disease)
    • Haem (anaemia, jaundice)
    • Immune (sepsis)
    • Eyes (ROP)
    • Temperature (hypothermia)
    • Skin (fragile).
  • Antenatal interventions that improve outcome: corticosteroids (↓ RDS, IVH, NEC, death)
    • magnesium sulfate (<30 wks: ↓ cerebral palsy)
    • antibiotics for PPROM (erythromycin)
    • delivery in a centre with NICU
    • delayed cord clamping
    • keep warm (plastic bag).

los.text: Identify the causes and management of common intrauterine, intrapartum and neonatal infections
los.html:
TimingInfectionNotes
Intrauterine (congenital, "TORCH")
  • Toxoplasma (cats/undercooked meat: hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification, chorioretinitis)
  • Rubella (cataract, deafness, PDA)
  • CMV (commonest congenital infection: microcephaly, sensorineural deafness, periventricular calcification; valganciclovir)
  • HSV
  • Syphilis (snuffles, rash, hepatosplenomegaly; benzylpenicillin)
  • Parvovirus B19 (fetal anaemia, hydrops)
  • VZV (limb hypoplasia, scarring)
  • HIV
  • Zika (microcephaly)
Screening in pregnancy: HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis
Intrapartum
  • Group B Streptococcus (commonest cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis)
  • E. coli
  • HSV (neonatal herpes: disseminated/encephalitis)
  • Hepatitis B
  • HIV
  • Chlamydia (conjunctivitis, pneumonia)
  • Gonorrhoea (ophthalmia neonatorum)
GBS risk: previous GBS baby, GBS bacteriuria/swab, preterm labour, PROM >18 h, maternal fever/chorioamnionitis → intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin
NeonatalEarly-onset sepsis (<72 h): GBS, E. coli, Listeria. Late-onset (>72 h): coagulase-negative staph (lines), S. aureus, gram-negatives, Candida; meningitisPreterms, lines, prolonged stay
Neonatal sepsis features(non-specific)Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, apnoeas, respiratory distress, tachycardia, jaundice, hypoglycaemia, seizures.
Management (NICE NG195)
  • Risk factors + clinical indicators → blood cultures, CRP, ± LP → IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin (early onset)
  • Late onset per local guideline (e.g. flucloxacillin/cefotaxime + gentamicin; amoxicillin + cefotaxime for meningitis)
  • Review at 36 h.
Prevention
  • Maternal screening and treatment
  • Vaccination (pertussis, influenza, RSV in pregnancy)
  • Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS
  • Hepatitis B vaccine ± HBIG at birth
  • HIV PMTCT (ART, mode of delivery, infant prophylaxis, avoid breastfeeding in UK)
  • Aciclovir/caesarean for primary genital herpes near term
  • Hand hygiene and line care in NICU.

los.text: Link definitions of prematurity and the impact of premature birth on health in infancy, childhood and later life
los.html:
Definitions (WHO)
  • Preterm = birth <37+0 weeks.
  • Extremely preterm <28, very preterm 28–31+6, moderate to late preterm 32–36+6.
  • Low birthweight <2,500 g
  • Very low <1,500 g
  • Extremely low <1,000 g. ~8% of UK births are preterm.
Impact in infancy
  • Neonatal mortality (prematurity is the leading cause of death in under-5s globally)
  • NICU morbidities (RDS, IVH, NEC, sepsis, BPD, ROP)
  • Feeding difficulties
  • Readmissions (RSV bronchiolitis).
Childhood
  • Neurodevelopmental impairment inversely related to gestation: cerebral palsy
  • Cognitive impairment/learning difficulties
  • ADHD, autism
  • Anxiety
  • Motor coordination problems
  • Visual impairment (ROP, strabismus)
  • Hearing loss
  • Chronic lung disease/asthma
  • Poor growth
  • School difficulties (even in moderate/late preterm).
  • NICE: developmental follow-up to 2 years (corrected age) for <30 weeks.
Later life (DOHaD: developmental origins of health and disease; Barker hypothesis)↑ hypertension, cardiovascular disease, insulin resistance/T2DM, CKD (fewer nephrons), reduced lung function/COPD, psychiatric disorders, lower educational attainment and income.
Corrected ageUse for developmental assessment and growth charts until ~2 years.

los.text: Describe the impact of premature birth on families
los.html:
Emotional
  • Shock
  • Grief for the expected birth
  • Anxiety (survival, disability)
  • Guilt (mothers blaming themselves)
  • Helplessness
  • Loss of control
  • Parental PTSD, postnatal depression (both parents)
  • Strain on relationships.
Bonding/attachment
  • Separation in NICU, limited ability to hold/feed
  • Promoted by kangaroo (skin-to-skin) care, family-integrated care (parents as primary caregivers in NICU), breastfeeding/expressing support.
Practical/financial
  • Long hospital stays
  • Travel and parking costs
  • Time off work
  • Care of siblings
  • Accommodation (Ronald McDonald houses)
  • Statutory leave issues (Neonatal Care Leave and Pay, from April 2025 in UK).
SiblingsDisruption, jealousy, anxiety.
After discharge
  • Home oxygen, feeding support, many appointments, fear of infection, ongoing uncertainty about development
  • Caring for a child with disability (long-term impact on careers, finances, mental health).
Support
  • Neonatal psychology
  • Bliss charity
  • Peer support groups
  • Neonatal outreach nurses
  • Palliative and bereavement care if the baby dies
  • Clear and compassionate communication
  • Involvement in ward rounds and decisions.

los.text: Interact with clinicians and families of ex-premature children
los.html:
Expert forum (interactive session)Hear from clinicians (neonatologists, neonatal nurses, follow-up teams) and families of children born prematurely. No specific factual LO.
Prompts to reflect on
  • What was the family's experience of NICU: communication, decision-making, uncertainty?
  • Long-term outcomes and needs of the child (development, education, health).
  • How professionals support families (family-integrated care, psychology, follow-up clinics).
  • What made communication helpful or harmful?
Link toLO 13–14 (impact of prematurity on health and families), LO 10 (ethics at viability).

los.text: Demonstrate the ability to take a comprehensive and sensitive sexual history from a patient using appropriate communication skills
sessions: Sexual history taking and shared decision making/exploitation
los.html:
Setting
  • Private, confidential
  • Explain why questions are asked and that they're routine
  • Offer chaperone
  • Non-judgemental, gender-neutral language
  • Avoid assumptions about sexual orientation/gender identity.
Structure
  • PC/HPC: symptoms (discharge, dysuria, ulcers/lumps, rash, pelvic/testicular pain, dyspareunia, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding), onset, duration.
  • Sexual history: last sexual intercourse (LSI) and previous partners (usually last 3 months): gender of partner(s), type of sex (oral, vaginal, anal; insertive/receptive), condom use, partner's symptoms/risk (from high-prevalence area, MSM, injecting drugs, paid sex), regular vs casual, contactability (for partner notification).
  • Previous STIs and tests, HIV/hepatitis testing, PrEP use, vaccination (hepatitis B, HPV, mpox).
  • Contraception and LMP/pregnancy risk; cervical screening history.
  • PMH, drug history, allergies, alcohol/recreational drugs (chemsex).
  • Safeguarding: age (<16? <13 = statutory child protection), consent, coercion, exploitation, domestic abuse, sexual assault, age gap/power imbalance, CSE indicators, FGM.
Shared decision-makingDiscuss testing options (NAAT chlamydia/gonorrhoea, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis), treatment, partner notification, contraception, PEP/PrEP; respect patient choices; confirm understanding.
Summarise and safety-net.

los.text: Identify and apply safeguarding principles within the context of a clinical consultation, recognizing potential signs of abuse or risk
sessions: Sexual history taking and shared decision making/exploitation
los.html:
Recognise
  • Under-16s in sexual relationships (under 13 cannot legally consent → always safeguarding referral)
  • Significant age difference/power imbalance
  • Coercion or control
  • Gifts/money/drugs/accommodation for sex (child sexual exploitation)
  • Frequent STIs or pregnancies/terminations
  • Multiple partners
  • Older "boyfriend"
  • Going missing
  • Drug/alcohol use
  • Self-harm
  • Injuries
  • Partner attending and answering for patient
  • Vulnerable adults (learning disability, mental capacity)
  • Domestic abuse indicators
  • FGM
  • Trafficking.
Fraser guidelines(contraception for <16 without parental involvement)
  • Understands advice
  • Can't be persuaded to inform parents
  • Likely to have sex anyway
  • Physical/mental health likely to suffer without it
  • in their best interests.
  • Gillick competence for consent to treatment generally.
Use toolsSpotting the Signs (BASHH/Brook proforma) for under-18s.
Act
  • Listen
  • Don't promise absolute confidentiality
  • Document
  • Discuss with safeguarding lead
  • Refer to social services ± police (Wales Safeguarding Procedures) where there is risk of significant harm
  • Information can be shared without consent when necessary to protect.
  • Adults at risk: adult safeguarding referral
  • MARAC for high-risk domestic abuse (DASH risk assessment).

los.text: Demonstrate the ability to perform a structured ophthalmological examination efficiently and accurately, applying appropriate techniques within a time-constrained setting.
los.html:
Visual acuity
  • Snellen chart at 6 m (or 3 m chart), each eye separately with glasses
  • Pinhole if reduced (improves refractive error)
  • Record e.g. 6/9
  • Count fingers/hand movements/perception of light if very poor
  • Near vision.
InspectionLids (ptosis), pupils (size, symmetry), redness, proptosis, squint, scars.
PupilsDirect and consensual light reflex, swinging light test (RAPD), accommodation.
Visual fieldsConfrontation (each eye, four quadrants, with red pin for central/blind spot), check for neglect/inattention.
Eye movements"H" pattern, ask about diplopia, look for nystagmus; cover test for squint.
Colour visionIshihara plates (optic neuritis).
Fundoscopy
  • Dim room
  • Dilate if needed (tropicamide)
  • Red reflex first
  • Then disc (colour, cup-to-disc ratio, margins: papilloedema)
  • Vessels (AV nipping, emboli)
  • Four quadrants
  • Macula last (ask to look at the light).
AdditionalFluorescein + blue light (corneal abrasion/ulcer), slit lamp, IOP, Amsler grid (macula).
Present conciselyAcuities, pupils, fields, movements, fundi, then summary and differential.
Time-constrained (OSCE)Practise a fixed order; explain each step; wash hands; thank patient.

los.text: Formulate differential diagnoses for a range of common and important ophthalmological presentations
los.html:
Sudden painless lossCRAO, CRVO, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, wet AMD, ischaemic optic neuropathy (GCA), stroke/TIA (amaurosis fugax).
Painful red eye with reduced visionAcute angle-closure glaucoma, anterior uveitis, keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis.
Red eye with normal visionConjunctivitis, episcleritis, subconjunctival haemorrhage.
Gradual visual lossCataract, dry AMD, chronic open-angle glaucoma, diabetic maculopathy, refractive error.
Double visionCN III/IV/VI palsy (diabetes, aneurysm: painful pupil-involving III = posterior communicating artery aneurysm), myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, orbital fracture, INO (MS).
Swollen optic discsPapilloedema (↑ ICP: tumour, IIH, venous sinus thrombosis), optic neuritis (papillitis), malignant hypertension.
Flashes and floatersPosterior vitreous detachment vs retinal tear/detachment.
Visual field defectsChiasmal (pituitary), homonymous (stroke), arcuate (glaucoma).
ChildrenSquint (refer: amblyopia), absent red reflex (cataract, retinoblastoma), orbital cellulitis.
ApproachOnset, pain, redness, discharge, unilateral/bilateral, systemic (headache, jaw claudication, diabetes, HTN), then exam findings narrow the list.

los.text: List key components required when taking a comprehensive paediatric history.
los.html:
• Presenting complaint and HPC (often from parent/carer and the child: use child's own words).
  • Birth history: gestation, birthweight, mode of delivery, complications, NICU admission, neonatal jaundice; antenatal history (scans, infections, maternal illness/medications).
  • Feeding/nutrition: breast/bottle, weaning, current diet, weight gain.
  • Growth and development: milestones (gross motor, fine motor/vision, speech/hearing, social), school performance, red book (growth charts).
  • Immunisations (up to date per UK schedule).
  • PMH: illnesses, hospital admissions, surgery.
  • Drug history and allergies (doses by weight).
  • Family history: consanguinity, inherited conditions, sudden deaths, siblings' health.
  • Social history: who lives at home
    • parental relationship/occupations
    • who has parental responsibility
    • housing
    • smoking
    • school/nursery
    • social services involvement (safeguarding: child protection plan?)
    • pets
    • travel.
  • Systems review relevant to age.
  • ICE of both child and parent.
  • Adolescents: HEEADSSS, see alone.

los.text: Apply appropriate communication strategies to manage a triadic consultation with a child and their parent or carer.
los.html:
Triadic consultationClinician + child + parent/carer.
Strategies
  • Introduce yourself to both; establish relationships (who is this adult? parental responsibility).
  • Engage the child first and directly at their developmental level (play, toys, simple language, sit at their level); let them tell their story where possible, then clarify with the parent.
  • Balance voices: avoid talking "over" the child; acknowledge parent's concerns and expertise.
  • Use age-appropriate explanations; check understanding with both.
  • Observe parent–child interaction (may give safeguarding clues).
  • Manage disagreements (child's wishes vs parent's views) sensitively; Gillick competence for older children.
  • For adolescents: offer time alone (confidentiality and its limits), explore sensitive issues.
  • Explore ICE of both parties; shared decision-making; agree a plan understandable to both.
ChallengesShy/anxious child, distressed parent, conflicting accounts, language barriers (avoid child as interpreter), safeguarding concerns.

los.text: Analyse history findings to formulate a reasoned differential diagnosis for urinary frequency in a paediatric patient.
los.html:
• Key differentials for urinary frequency in a child:
DiagnosisHistory clues
UTIDysuria, fever, foul-smelling urine, abdominal/loin pain, new wetting; infants: fever, vomiting, poor feeding
Type 1 diabetesPolyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, tiredness, nocturia/new bedwetting, (DKA: vomiting, abdominal pain, breathlessness) → urgent same-day capillary glucose
ConstipationInfrequent hard stools, straining, soiling; rectal loading presses on bladder
Overactive bladder / daytime wettingUrgency, holding manoeuvres, small frequent voids
Diabetes insipidusLarge volumes of dilute urine, intense thirst (craves water)
Psychogenic polydipsia / habitDrinks excessively; stress
Pollakiuria (extraordinary daytime frequency)Very frequent small voids, no nocturia, often after stressful event; self-limiting
Renal tract abnormality, VUR, renal diseaseRecurrent UTIs, poor growth, HTN
Sexual abuse / vulvovaginitis / threadwormsDysuria, genital irritation, behavioural change: consider safeguarding
Hypercalciuria, drugs (diuretics), caffeine
Reasoning
  • Frequency + polydipsia + weight loss → T1DM (don't miss)
  • with dysuria/fever → UTI
  • with constipation → treat bowels
  • Daytime only, no systemic features → functional.
Next steps
  • Urine dipstick (glucose, ketones, nitrites, leucocytes) and MSU culture, capillary glucose, abdominal exam, growth/BP, constipation assessment
  • Renal USS if recurrent/atypical UTI.
